title: The Color Missing From Your Indoor Lighting
hook: Indigo light is abundant in sunlight and largely absent from indoor LEDs. In tree shrews, adding it back completely prevented nearsightedness.
key_points: Indigo light sits between blue and violet and is largely missing from indoor LED lighting.
In tree shrews, indigo light completely prevented myopia from developing.
Tree shrew eyes share important similarities with human eyes.
Childhood myopia rates have risen sharply alongside more time spent indoors.
Time outdoors is already the best-supported protection against childhood myopia.
The finding hints indoor lighting could be redesigned to mimic sunlight's spectrum.
content_html: Childhood nearsightedness has climbed steeply over the past few decades, and the single most reliable protective factor found so far isn't screen limits or reading posture — it's time spent outdoors. Nobody is certain why. The leading suspicion is light: outdoor light is far brighter than indoor light, and its spectrum is different.
extra_html:
This study points to a specific missing ingredient. Indigo light, the band between blue and violet, is abundant in sunlight and largely absent from indoor LEDs. In tree shrews — small mammals whose eyes are close enough to human eyes to be a standard model for myopia research — indigo light completely prevented myopia from developing.

That's a striking result and still an animal one. Tree shrew eyes are similar to ours, not identical, and "prevented in a controlled lab exposure" is a long way from "works in a classroom." The intriguing implication is that indoor lighting might be redesigned to include the wavelengths sunlight has and LEDs dropped, which would be an unusually painless public health intervention. Until that's tested in children, the advice that already has evidence behind it stands: get kids outside.

related.title: Protecting Your Eyes
related.hook: Some of the most serious eye diseases, like glaucoma, steal sight silently with no early symptoms. A regular eye exam is often the only way to catch them in time.

flashcards.prompt: What was the effect of indigo light on myopia in tree shrews?
flashcards.back_html: It completely prevented myopia from developing. Indigo is plentiful in sunlight and largely missing from indoor LEDs.

flashcards.prompt: Why is this finding a plausible piece of the childhood myopia story?

choices.text: Myopia has risen alongside more time indoors, where indigo light is scarce
Indigo light strengthens the muscles that focus the lens
LED bulbs emit more indigo light than sunlight does

flashcards.explanation_html: Time outdoors is the best-supported protection against childhood myopia. A wavelength that is abundant outside and scarce inside is a candidate for why.

flashcards.prompt: What should a parent actually do with this?
flashcards.back_html: Nothing new yet — this is animal work. The existing, well-supported advice stands: more time outdoors for children.
